lead: Under a steady DC magnetic field, a ferrite in a waveguide treats the two travel directions differently. A wave going one way is rotated, passed or delayed differently from a wave going back. Three devices use this: the isolator (passes one way, absorbs the other), the circulator (hands power round ports in fixed rotation), and the nonreciprocal phase shifter. They sit at radar front ends, transmitters and phased arrays.
prereq: You need 4.1 S-parameters for port waves and the scattering matrix, and Unit 1 for waveguide propagation and phase constant β.

sections.h3: Ferrite under DC bias: rotation that does not undo itself

blocks.text: A ferrite is an insulating ceramic of iron oxide with other metal oxides. It has low microwave loss. In a waveguide it is a rod, disc or toroid placed where the wave's magnetic field is strongest.

With no magnet a ferrite is just a dielectric. A steady DC magnetic field along the rod makes electron spins precess. The permeability becomes a tensor, and its value depends on whether the wave's magnetic field rotates clockwise or anticlockwise about the bias.
A linearly polarised wave is two counter-rotating circular waves. In biased ferrite they travel at different speeds, so the plane of polarisation turns on exit. This is Faraday rotation.

blocks.where: θ is rotation angle in radians, V is the Verdet constant of the material in rad/(T·m), B is DC flux density in tesla, and L is ferrite length in metres.

blocks.text: The bias sets the rotation sense, not the travel direction. A wave 1→2 turns by +θ; reflected 2→1 it turns by +θ again, giving 2θ, not zero. That is nonreciprocity. A reciprocal part such as plain waveguide undoes its effect on return.

sections.h3: The Y-junction circulator and its S-matrix

blocks.text: A circulator sends power round its ports in fixed rotation. The three-port form is a Y junction: three waveguides at 120°, or three striplines on ferrite, with a ferrite post at the centre and a small permanent magnet across it.

In the junction the biased ferrite supports two counter-rotating modes with different phase constants. Their sum bulges towards one arm. Power in at port 1 goes to port 2, port 2 to port 3, port 3 to port 1. Flip the magnet and the rotation reverses.

blocks.where: row index is output port, column index is input port, so S₂₁ = 1 means a wave in at port 1 comes out at port 2; S₃₂ = 1 and S₁₃ = 1 carry the rotation 2→3→1. The zeros are isolated paths. φ is insertion phase. The ideal matrix is matched and lossless but not symmetric, because S₂₁ = 1 while S₁₂ = 0.

blocks.text: A good waveguide circulator has insertion loss under 1 dB and isolation 20 dB or more over one waveguide band.
A four-port circulator circulates 1→2→3→4→1. It is used as a radar duplexer sharing one antenna between transmitter and receiver (Unit 6), and to separate incident and reflected waves at a load.

sections.h3: Isolator: a circulator with a matched load

blocks.text: Terminate port 3 of a three-port circulator in a matched load: that is an isolator, a two-port passing power one way and absorbing it the other way.

Forward, port 1 → port 2, the loss is insertion loss IL, so P₂ = P₁ − IL. Reverse, power enters port 2 and is circulated to port 3, where the matched load absorbs it; only the circulator's leakage reaches port 1. That reverse transmission from port 2 to port 1 is the isolation I, and it equals the 1→3 leakage of the same circulator. With IL = 0.5 dB, I = 25 dB and input 10 dBm, port 2 carries 9.5 dBm and port 3 sees −15 dBm.
The load must stay matched. A reflection from port 3 comes back in at port 3 and circulates 3→1, straight into the port supposed to be isolated, so a poor load destroys isolation.
Isolators sit between transmitter and antenna, so a mismatch or arc reflects nothing into the source, and before low-noise receivers or parametric amplifiers that must not see a transmitter pulse.
A phase shifter adds a known phase φ. Reciprocal designs give the same φ both ways: a dielectric slab slid across the guide, switched line lengths using PIN diodes, or a loaded line.

blocks.where: φ is phase shift in radians, β is phase constant of the biased ferrite section in rad/m, β₀ is phase constant of the empty guide in rad/m, and L is ferrite length in metres.

blocks.text: A DC coil sets the bias, the bias sets β, so coil current sets phase shift: beam steering with no moving parts (Unit 3). Because bias acts differently on the two directions, forward and reverse shifts differ. In a reflection-type phase shifter, port 2 of a circulator is closed by a short-circuited phase shifter: forward φ_f, reflection adds 180°, return reverse φ_r, leave port 3 with φ_f + 180° + φ_r.
A gyrator is the abstract two-port version with 180° differential phase shift between directions; the ferrite circulator is its microwave form.

figure.caption: Forward power 1→2 leaves at 9.5 dBm. Port 3 is isolated from port 1 by 25 dB, so only −15 dBm of leakage arrives there; the matched load absorbs it and nothing returns to port 1.

spec.title: Three-port circulator used as an isolator
spec.aria: Three-port circulator: forward power 1→2 leaves port 2 at 9.5 dBm after 0.5 dB loss. Port 3 is isolated by 25 dB, so only −15 dBm leakage arrives; the matched load absorbs it and nothing returns to port 1.

examples.question: A three-port circulator circulates 1→2→3→1. Port 3 is terminated in a matched load, so ports 1 and 2 work as an isolator. Forward insertion loss is 0.5 dB and reverse isolation is 25 dB. A signal of 10 dBm enters port 1. Find (a) power leaving port 2 and (b) power reaching port 3.
steps: Port 3 receives only leakage against circulation, attenuated by isolation: P₃ = 10 − 25 = −15 dBm.
The matched load absorbs this −15 dBm. No reflection returns to port 1, so isolation holds.
Check: 9.5 dBm = 8.91 mW and −15 dBm = 0.032 mW, about 280:1, the 24.5 dB gap.
examples.answer: P₂ = 9.5 dBm and P₃ = −15 dBm: ports 1 and 2 form an isolator with 0.5 dB forward loss and 25 dB reverse isolation.
examples.check:
p1_dbm = 10
insertion_loss_db = 0.5
isolation_db = 25
p2_dbm = p1_dbm - insertion_loss_db
p3_dbm = p1_dbm - isolation_db
print(p2_dbm)
print(p3_dbm)

traps: Drawing circulation arrows the wrong way. Read the arrow on the device, or remember that reversing the DC magnet reverses 1→2→3 into 1→3→2.
Treating an isolator as reciprocal. Its scattering matrix is not symmetric: S₂₁ ≈ 1, S₁₂ ≈ 0. Never assume its loss works both ways.
Leaving unused circulator ports open. An open port reflects, the reflection circulates into the isolated port, and measured isolation collapses.

Confusing isolation with return loss. Isolation is reverse transmission (S₁₂ in dB). Return loss is reflection at one port, quoted as a positive dB figure: return loss = −20 log₁₀|S₁₁|, so S₁₁ = −20 dB means 20 dB return loss.
Unit slips in dB. For power use 10 log₁₀, subtract dB losses; 25 dB isolation means leakage is 1/316, not 1/25.

quiz.q: In a three-port circulator, power enters port 1. Where does it leave, and which direction is isolated?
quiz.a: Port 2. Power circulates 1→2→3→1, so 1→3 is isolated.

quiz.q: Define insertion loss and isolation of an isolator.
quiz.a: Insertion loss = forward attenuation in dB (about 0.5 dB). Isolation = reverse attenuation in dB (20–30 dB).

quiz.q: Why is biased ferrite nonreciprocal while plain dielectric is not?
quiz.a: The DC bias makes permeability a tensor, so the two counter-rotating circular components see different permeability. Faraday rotation sense is set by bias, not travel direction, so a round trip rotates 2θ, not zero. A dielectric changes phase constant equally both ways.

quiz.q: Why must the load at port 3 of a circulator-based isolator be well matched?
quiz.a: A reflection at port 3 circulates 3→1 into the isolated port, adding to leakage and reducing measured isolation even if the circulator is perfect.

quiz.q: A three-port circulator has 0.6 dB insertion loss and 30 dB isolation. A 100 mW (20 dBm) signal enters port 1; port 3 is matched. Find output at port 2 and leakage at port 3.
quiz.a: P₂ = 20 − 0.6 = 19.4 dBm = 87.1 mW. P₃ = 20 − 30 = −10 dBm = 0.1 mW. The load absorbs 0.1 mW.

quiz.q: A circulator has port 2 closed by a short-circuited nonreciprocal phase shifter with 90° forward and 70° reverse. A signal enters port 1. Where does it exit and with what total phase?
quiz.a: 1→2 gives 90°; the short adds 180°; the reverse pass adds 70°; it leaves port 3 with 90 + 180 + 70 = 340° (−20°).

quiz.q: Can an isolator be built from reciprocal components only? Justify.
quiz.a: No. In a reciprocal network S₂₁ = S₁₂, so reverse attenuation also attenuates the forward path equally. Breaking symmetry needs a nonreciprocal element, normally a DC-biased ferrite, or an active device.

quiz.q: A radar uses a three-port circulator: transmitter port 1, antenna port 2, receiver port 3. What does each port see for the transmitted pulse and for the echo?
quiz.a: Transmit: 1→2 to the antenna; port 3 gets only isolation-level leakage, handled by a limiter. Echo: returns into 2 and circulates 2→3 to the receiver; port 1 gets only leakage.

beyond: Not for exam. Self-biased hexaferrite circulators remove the magnet and suit millimetre-wave 5G arrays. Yttrium iron garnet spheres tuned by a coil make wideband tunable oscillators and filters because ferrite resonance rises with bias. Faraday rotation also makes optical isolators for fibre lasers. Research pushes biased ferrite into spin-wave and magnonic logic. Search: self-biased circulator, YIG tuned oscillator, Faraday rotator.
